extracted.intended_audience: agency attorneys, rulewriters, and policymakers involved in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for federal agencies on legal obligations and best practices for soliciting, considering, and responding to public comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act and related statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to submit comments and consideration of relevant matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Administrative Procedure Act, agencies must give interested persons the opportunity to submit comments on proposed rules. Agencies must consider the 'relevant matter presented' in those comments before finalizing the proposed rules. (5 U.S.C. § 553(c))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the baseline procedural obligation: publish notice, permit comment, and consider relevant material submitted during the comment period. See IIB-014 for additional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to respond to significant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies finalize proposed rules, they must 'respond to significant comments received during the period for public comment.' (Perez v. Mortg. Bankers Ass’n (2015))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other statutes may also require agencies to explain how they addressed comments (for example, explain changes made in response to comments in initial Regulatory Flexibility Act analyses (5 U.S.C. § 604(a)(2))). Agencies therefore should identify which comments are 'significant' and ensure a substantive response in the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to respond to significant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s failure to respond to significant comments renders the final rule arbitrary and capricious and subject to being 'held unlawful and set aside.' (Ohio v. EPA (2024); 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts ordinarily vacate the rule and remand it to the agency to correct the procedural error, though courts sometimes allow the rule to remain in effect (remand without vacatur) if the agency can likely justify the decision on remand and vacatur would be disruptive. (Am. Bankers Ass’n v. NCUA (D.C. Cir. 2019); ACUS Rec. 2013-6)

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining whether a comment is 'significant'
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining whether a rulemaking comment is significant is a fact-dependent inquiry. Agencies must respond to comments that 'raise points relevant to the agency’s decision and which, if adopted, would require a change in an agency proposed rule.' (Nat’l Shooting Sports Found., Inc. v. Jones (D.C. Cir. 2013))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are not required to respond to comments that are not material to the proceeding or that are overly speculative or cryptic. (Direct Communs. Cedar Valley, LLC v. FCC (10th Cir. 2014); Oakbrook Land Holdings, LLC v. Comm’r (6th Cir. 2022)). Agencies should evaluate significance on a comment-by-comment basis, focusing on relevance and the potential to change the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of agency responses — explain major issues and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: When responding to significant comments, agencies must explain their decisions in a manner that enables courts 'to see what major issues of policy were ventilated . . . and why the agency reacted to them as it did.' (Bloomberg, LP v. SEC (D.C. Cir. 2022))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess the adequacy of responses using the familiar arbitrary-and-capricious review factors: whether the agency addressed important aspects of the problem and offered explanations consistent with the evidence before the agency. Agencies should provide reasoned explanations and, where appropriate, tie responses to the administrative record. (See Ohio v. Becerra (6th Cir. 2023) example addressing consistency with similar federal law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide adequate notice to enable meaningful comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Before responding to comments, agencies must first ensure that their proposed rules provide adequate notice of the issues to enable interested persons to comment meaningfully on the rule. (Nat’l Lifeline Ass’n v. FCC (D.C. Cir. 2019))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate notice may require making supporting materials—such as studies, reports, and data—available to the public to support the comment process. (See IIB-005.) If the public did not have adequate notice of an issue, comments on that issue may be less effective as a basis for defending the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure final rule is a 'logical outgrowth' of the proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts generally require final rules to represent the 'logical outgrowth' of proposed rules so that members of the public are not deprived of the opportunity to comment on matters ultimately addressed in the final rule. (Long Island Care at Home, Ltd. v. Coke (2007))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should ensure that substantive changes in the final rule were reasonably foreseeable from the notice so that commenters had an opportunity to respond; otherwise courts may find the rule procedurally defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate length of comment periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider the appropriate length of comment periods to allow meaningful public participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS has issued recommendations (ACUS Rec. 2011-2) about comment period length; agencies should weigh complexity of the proposal, need for information, and practical constraints when setting comment deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of comments after the initial public comment period
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider when to accept comments after the initial public comment period has ended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS Rec. 2011-2 addresses acceptance of late submissions; agencies may accept late comments in appropriate circumstances, balancing fairness, the integrity of the record, and administrative efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementing notice-and-comment with RFIs and ANPRMs
rubrics_metrics.description: In some circumstances agencies should supplement the notice-and-comment process by soliciting comments via requests for information (RFIs) and advance notices of proposed rulemaking (ANPRMs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS Rec. 2018-7 recommends using RFIs and ANPRMs to broaden engagement and gather information prior to formal notice-and-comment, particularly for complex or novel regulatory issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing mass, computer-generated, and falsely attributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should address how to manage mass submissions, computer-generated, and falsely attributed comments during the public comment process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS Rec. 2021-1 provides recommendations on identifying, sorting, and responding to mass or machine-generated comment campaigns and to comments that may be falsely attributed, so agencies can focus on substantive input while maintaining a reliable administrative record.
